```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
library(igraph)
set.seed(42)
```

## Adjacency Matrices

An **adjacency matrix** \( A \) of a graph records who is connected to whom:

$$
A_{ij} = 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if there is an edge from } i \text{ to } j \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

Nothing forces $A_{ij} = A_{ji}$. A directed edge can exist in one direction only. That is the technical starting point: relationships need not be symmetric.

## Directed graph (asymmetric)

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-cap: "A small directed graph and its (non-symmetric) adjacency matrix"
#| code-fold: true
#| 

g <- igraph::graph_from_literal(1-+2, 1-+3, 2-+3, 3-+4, 4-+2, 2-+1)
A <- igraph::as_adjacency_matrix(g, sparse = FALSE)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(g, vertex.color = "lightblue", vertex.size = 24, edge.arrow.size = 0.8,
     main = "Directed graph")
graphics::image(t(A[nrow(A):1, ]), axes = FALSE, col = c("white", "steelblue"),
      main = "Adjacency matrix A")
graphics::box()

```

```{r}
#| echo: false
print(A)
```

## Undirected graph (forced symmetry)

When every edge is mutual we obtain an undirected graph. Its adjacency matrix satisfies \( A = A^\top \) — the matrix is equal to its own transpose (its “mirror”).

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-cap: "The same vertices made undirected: A becomes symmetric"
#| code-fold: true
#| 

g_und <- as.undirected(g, mode = "collapse")
A_und <- as_adjacency_matrix(g_und, sparse = FALSE)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(g_und, vertex.color = "lightgreen", main = "Undirected graph")
image(t(A_und[nrow(A_und):1, ]), axes = FALSE, col = c("white", "darkgreen"),
      main = "Symmetric adjacency matrix")
box()
```

## p5.js: draw directed vs. mutual links

```{=html}
<div id="graph-sketch"></div>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/p5@1.9.0/lib/p5.min.js"></script>
<script>
new p5((p) => {
  let nodes = [];
  let edges = [];
  p.setup = () => {
    p.createCanvas(500, 350);
    for (let i = 0; i < 6; i++) {
      nodes.push(p.createVector(80 + i * 70, 180 + p.random(-40, 40)));
    }
  };
  p.draw = () => {
    p.background(250);
    // directed edges
    p.stroke(180, 80, 80);
    p.strokeWeight(1.5);
    for (let e of edges) {
      let a = nodes[e.from], b = nodes[e.to];
      p.line(a.x, a.y, b.x, b.y);
      // arrow head
      let ang = p.atan2(b.y - a.y, b.x - a.x);
      p.push();
      p.translate(b.x, b.y);
      p.rotate(ang);
      p.line(0, 0, -8, -4);
      p.line(0, 0, -8, 4);
      p.pop();
    }
    // nodes
    p.noStroke();
    p.fill(100, 150, 220);
    for (let n of nodes) p.circle(n.x, n.y, 18);
  };
  p.mousePressed = () => {
    // add a random directed edge
    let i = p.floor(p.random(nodes.length));
    let j = p.floor(p.random(nodes.length));
    if (i !== j) edges.push({from: i, to: j});
  };
}, document.getElementById("graph-sketch"));
</script>
<p><em>Click to add directed edges. Nothing forces the reverse edge to exist.</em></p>
```

## Why This Matters for Design

In the real world most relations are directed or only partially mutual:  
influence, gaze, citation, one-way streets, “follows” on a social network.  
The adjacency matrix records that asymmetry without apology.  

The next document asks what happens when we *idealize* the situation and demand that every relationship be perfectly mirrored.
